summary: All 132 supplied occurrences were reviewed. I 1 includes assertive oaths, binding promises and adjuration; III 1 adds a causer. No new numbered sense is warranted.

Valency: b- gives the oath authority; l- gives the recipient in Infectum and Imperativ; aʕle gives the person adjured at 82/67. With Preterit, l-marked full NPs can instead identify the swearer, e.g. lu taʕlo at PrS 75/18, 34, 131 and la tre qaṭune at PrS 59/40. The l-marked swearer must not be mistaken for an oath recipient.

Performative Infectum coexists with habitual use, dependent yome/yomət, prospective gədyomeno and coercive Gədyomət. Preterit imeli can express a past oath still binding now (PrS 75/37, 81/87). Conditional Gyomət at 65/90 has no -wa and remains Infectum.

Imanat is a cognate oath noun (54/23; 61/144), not an additional finite occurrence or automatically an idiomatic phrase. No new light-verb collocation is established. Ingressive səmle d yome at JL 17.6/10 concerns sym, not a lexical ymy idiom.

Existing I Imperativ examples legitimately include accompanying Infectum yomeno in their quoted exchanges; this does not justify moving the entire examples. Existing III Infectum at 89/124 is retained pending form assessment.

At 111/92 alignment is explicitly partial; its translation was not quoted. At PrS 73/64 verse_translation stops before the oath although context_translation continues; no example is added from that continuation.

Read both round-1 files before the Jan occurrence. Round 1 retains one broad I sense for oaths and adjuration, and a separate III sense for causing another to swear. Jan gives no clear semantic distinction or new government, and no new sense, idiom or gloss change is proposed.

Written ymeli in Jan 1.45/1959 contrasts with inherited imele and round-1 imeli. This is evidence of spelling/form variation, not by itself proof of a pronounced initial consonant, a different stem or a change in argument coding. Retain I Preterit provisionally.

The following umarno əlla huwweyo is the narrator’s identification of the suspected thief; the verse later repeats “my pistol”. The reader’s claim that the assertion identifies the owner is unsupported by the immediate wording. Oath content is inferred from this discourse, not assigned a newly attested complement marker. The later Alo formula is not treated as a separate ymy collocation.

Confirm the segmentation and person/gender marking of gyumallux (30/144), and compare female speech with Kyomenolux (59/47). The verses establish oath meaning but do not establish gender neutralization.
At 80/21, is bare Pir Kureš a complement or an independently quoted oath formula with omitted b-?

Check source pagination versus verse numbering: PrS 70/41 corresponds to the inherited prs 199/5 wording, and PrS 60/103 to the imele w mayəṯ formula. Are prs page references intentionally a separate system? Do not replace them automatically.

Verify inherited 55/20, 25 and 55/39 against supplied 55/21, 26 and 40. The aggregate references need not all cite the full imele w mayəṯ formula; 88/95 supplies an oath and threat, not those exact words.
Should Moméwulle at 89/124 remain III Infectum or be Imperativ? The editor's existing placement is retained.

JL 15.6/7 names the grandfather as causer; the v8 threat addresses the father. Retain the discourse mismatch. Should the forms/page material embedded in existing example ymy.III.t.preterit.1 be structurally separated?

Jan 1.45/1959: confirm ymeli as “I swore” and the value of its initial written y. Does any local usage support the alternative “I made him swear”, despite the absence here of an overt causee or the usual III form?
Does əlla huwweyo state the oath’s content or a separate assertion after the oath? The current example and sense do not require a new complementation rule.
Oath-takers include speaking animals in PrS narratives; reciprocal l ḥḏoḏe expresses mutual recipients without Detransitive morphology.
